source_observations: Stark Part 9 is explicitly marked ROUGH DRAFT (2010); retain its useful definitions/examples but do not rely on its unexplained or inconsistent formulations without repair and independent support.

The 2017 Lugosi–Mendelson estimator is defined using k = ceil(360 log(2/delta)) blocks, with the proof assuming nonempty blocks; the stated all-N claim has no construction when k > N. Scaffold only the range where the block construction is defined unless a repaired small-sample extension is proved.
The 2019 trimmed-mean source states delta >= exp(-N/4) for its univariate theorem; preserve this range condition and do not extend its guarantees to arbitrary confidence levels.

Cai–Zhou sparse covariance results assume sub-Gaussian observations, p at least n^beta for beta>1, 0<=q<1, and cn,p <= M n^((1-q)/2)(log p)^(-(3-q)/2); the robust Huber-contamination covariance theorem is a separate paper and does not inherit this theorem automatically.

Minsker–Wei use E||X-EX||^4<infinity and a matrix-truncated estimator, with a median-of-means location pilot and effective-rank-dependent operator-norm bounds; this is a heavy-tail moment model, not arbitrary Huber contamination.

Chen–Gao–Ren’s public full arXiv PDF includes the supplementary technical proof section; its covariance model is (1-epsilon)N(0,Sigma)+epsilon Q with arbitrary Q, epsilon<1/5 in the upper theorems, bounded spectral norm, and depth optimizers. The source explicitly states high-dimensional computation is challenging/theoretical and only supplies numerical methods for low/moderate dimensions.

Cai–Zhou’s author-hosted six-page supplement was downloaded after the Yale HTTPS host presented a self-signed/mismatched certificate; this retrieval note is retained in the acquisition manifest and will be disclosed in the dossier. The file is publicly linked from the author-hosted supplement citation and its full title/authors/content match the main paper’s DOI reference.

The Ronchetti Princeton-hosted lecture provides an independent full treatment of influence functions and finite-sample replacement breakdown definitions. It is an undated 41-slide lecture and does not contain full proofs of its asymptotic expansions or M-estimator formulas; use it for definitions and orientation, with proofs supplied or verified separately.
